books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs

stimulus.text: The lithograph, published in 1836, shows President Andrew Jackson at right, striking with a cane at a many-headed serpent. The serpent's heads carry the names of states, and the largest head is Nicholas Biddle, president of the Second Bank of the United States. The caption reads 'GENERAL JACKSON SLAYING THE MANY HEADED MONSTER.' In his veto of the Bank's recharter in 1832, Jackson wrote: 'It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.' He also wrote that the Court's opinion 'ought not to control the coordinate authorities of this Government,' and that 'the Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution.'
stimulus.source_note: Lithograph 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster,' Henry R. Robinson, 1836 (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Veto quotation: Andrew Jackson, veto message, July 10, 1832, public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The lithograph's image of the Bank as a many-headed monster most directly reflects the belief that the Bank

options.text: protected small farmers from the state banks' paper money
options.misconception: Farmers were Jackson's people, so it is easy to assume the Bank he attacked must have hurt them by helping someone else.

options.text: kept interest rates low for western settlers buying land
options.misconception: A bank's job is lending, so it is easy to frame the fight as a quarrel about interest rates.

options.text: put dangerous power over the nation's money in a few hands
refused to lend money to the federal government in wartime
options.misconception: A bank that fights a president looks stubborn, so it is easy to imagine it refused him money.

rationales.A: Jackson's supporters said the Bank served the rich, not small farmers, and the monster image attacks it rather than praising it.
rationales.B: Low rates for settlers were not the charge; the charge was that the Bank's power helped an elite at others' expense.
rationales.C: A monster with many heads, led by Biddle, pictures the Bank as a spreading power that served a privileged few.
rationales.D: The Bank lent to the government and held its deposits; refusing loans was never the charge against it.
rationales.general:
1. Name the monster. The serpent is the Second Bank, and its largest head is its president, Nicholas Biddle.
2. Ask what monsters do. A many-headed monster spreads its power everywhere, which is how Jackson's friends pictured the Bank's grip on money.
Background: in his veto message Jackson called the Bank a privilege for the rich and powerful.
Remember: when a cartoon turns an institution into a beast, ask whose power the beast is said to serve.

figures.caption: General Jackson slaying the many headed monster, 1836. Jackson strikes a serpent whose heads bear state names.
figures.alt: A lithograph of President Andrew Jackson striking a many-headed serpent with a cane; the serpent's heads carry state names and the largest head is Nicholas Biddle
